The network of camel caravan routes that carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa north to the Mediterranean, from roughly the 7th century BCE to the early centuries CE. The routes ran up the western side of Arabia to Gaza and Damascus, with branches to Mesopotamia.

Frankincense and myrrh are tree resins. Temples across the Mediterranean and the Middle East burned them by the ton, and they were used in medicine and embalming. Only a few dry regions grew the trees, so the kingdoms there grew rich: Saba, Qataban, Hadramaut and later Himyar. Saba's Marib Dam watered the oasis at the heart of this wealth. In the north the Nabataeans of Petra controlled the last stretch and taxed every load.

Demand peaked under the Roman Empire, and Roman writers grumbled about the gold flowing to Arabia. From the 1st century CE more goods went by ship up the Red Sea instead, and later Christian worship used far less incense. The land route faded, and with it the old kingdoms of south Arabia.
